title: Rights, Responsibilities and Illinois
bigQuestion: What does a citizen get from the government, what does a citizen owe, and how can one person make things fairer?

story.title: Room 12 Gets a Crosswalk
story.kicker: Four fourth graders, one dangerous street, and the eight steps it took to paint two white lines.
paragraphs: Every morning, Amara, Jonah, Luis and Kim crossed Oak Street to get to Lincoln Elementary. There was no crosswalk. Cars did not slow down. One rainy morning a pickup truck skidded and stopped a few feet from Jonah. He was fine, but he was shaking. That afternoon the four friends told their teacher, Mr. Bell. He said, "You have the right to ask for a change. Let's find out how."

Step one was finding out who was in charge of Oak Street. Kim looked it up. Oak Street belonged to the city, not the state. So the city council could fix it. Step two was gathering evidence. For a week the four stood at the corner before school with a clipboard. They counted cars and kids. They wrote down the numbers. About two hundred cars and sixty kids used that corner every morning.

Step three was a petition. They wrote one sentence at the top: "We ask the city to paint a crosswalk at Oak Street and School Lane." Then they asked people to sign. Parents signed. Neighbors signed. The school crossing guard signed. In two weeks they had one hundred forty names. Step four was a letter to their council member, Ms. Duarte. Amara wrote it. She put in the car count and a copy of the petition.

Step five was the meeting. Ms. Duarte invited them to speak at the city council. Luis was scared, but he read the numbers out loud. Jonah told about the truck. A council member asked how much a crosswalk would cost. The public works chief said about one thousand dollars for paint and two signs. Step six was waiting. Government is slow. Nothing happened for a month.

Step seven was following up. Kim wrote a polite note to Ms. Duarte asking about the crosswalk. Ms. Duarte answered that the council had voted yes. Step eight came on a Saturday in May. A city truck pulled up. Two workers painted thick white stripes across Oak Street and set a yellow sign on each side. The four friends stood on the sidewalk and watched. They had used their rights, done their homework, and changed their street.
story.think: Which of the eight steps do you think mattered most? What would have happened if the four had skipped the car count?

lessons.title: The Bill of Rights
lessons.mainIdea: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, and it lists things the government cannot take from you.
reading: A *right* is something you are allowed to do or have, and no one may take it away without a very good reason. In 1787, the people who wrote the U.S. Constitution set up the three branches of government. But many Americans said something was missing. Where was the list of rights the new government could never touch? They would not vote for the Constitution without one.

So in 1791 the states added ten changes to the Constitution. A change to the Constitution is called an *amendment*. Those first ten amendments together are called the *Bill of Rights*. Here the word "bill" means a list, not a plan for a law. The Bill of Rights protects your right to speak, to pray as you choose, to have a fair trial, and more.

The Bill of Rights is written as a list of things the government may not do. It says Congress shall make no law that stops free speech. It says no one may be punished without a fair trial. The writers had lived under a king who searched homes and jailed people who spoke against him. They wanted to make sure that could never happen again.

words.d: something you are allowed to do or have that cannot be taken away without a very good reason
a change added to the Constitution
the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, added in 1791

look.title: A List of Cannots
look.text: Imagine your school posted a list called "Rules for the Principal." It might say: The principal cannot read your private notes. The principal cannot keep you after school without telling you why. The principal cannot stop you from asking questions at assembly. That is a bill of rights for students.
look.prompt: Why might it be more important to list what a leader cannot do than what a student cannot do?

check.q: What is the Bill of Rights?
choices: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
A plan for a new law
A list of rules for students
The part of the Constitution that sets up Congress
check.why: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, added in 1791 to protect people from the government.

check.q: What is an amendment?
choices: A change added to the Constitution
check.why: An amendment is a change to the Constitution. The first ten are the Bill of Rights.

check.q: Why did many Americans want a Bill of Rights added?
choices: They wanted more branches of government
They wanted a list of rights the new government could never take away
check.why: They had lived under a king who jailed people for speaking. They wanted rights written down and protected.

lessons.title: Speaking and Believing
lessons.mainIdea: The First Amendment protects your freedom to speak, write, worship, gather and ask the government for change.
reading: When the four friends in the story wrote a petition, they were using the First Amendment. The First Amendment is short, but it packs in five freedoms. Freedom of *speech* means you may say what you think, even if the mayor or the president does not like it. Freedom of the *press* means newspapers and reporters may print the truth, even when it makes leaders look bad.

Freedom of *religion* has two parts. The government may not set up an official church for everyone. And the government may not stop you from praying or worshiping as you choose, or from choosing no religion at all. In a public school, a teacher cannot make you pray. But you may pray quietly on your own. Both parts protect you.

Freedom to *assemble* means people may gather peacefully, for a march or a meeting. The right to *petition* means you may ask the government to change something, and it may not punish you for asking. The four friends' one hundred forty signatures were a petition. Free speech does have limits. You may not lie to hurt someone or threaten to hurt a person. But sharing an opinion, even an unpopular one, is protected.

words.d: saying what you think; freedom of speech means the government cannot punish you for your opinion
newspapers, reporters and other news; freedom of the press protects their right to print the truth
a written request to the government, often signed by many people
to gather together peacefully, such as for a march or meeting

look.title: The First Amendment
look.text: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.
look.prompt: Find the five freedoms in this one sentence. Which one did the four friends use to get their crosswalk?

check.q: Which freedom did the four friends use when they collected signatures?
check.why: A petition is a written request to the government. The First Amendment protects the right to make one.

check.q: What does freedom of the press protect?
choices: Reporters' right to print the truth, even about leaders
The right to own a printing press
The right to a fair trial
The right to vote at eighteen
check.why: Freedom of the press means newspapers and reporters may report the truth without being punished by the government.

check.q: Which of these is NOT protected by freedom of speech?
choices: Saying the mayor is doing a bad job
Wearing a shirt with an opinion on it
Writing a letter against a new law
check.why: Free speech has limits. Threats and lies that hurt people are not protected. Opinions are.

lessons.title: A Fair Trial
lessons.mainIdea: If you are accused of a crime, the Bill of Rights promises a public trial, a jury, and the chance to defend yourself.
reading: Imagine a police officer says you stole a bike. You did not. What happens next? In some countries, you could sit in jail for years with no chance to explain. The Bill of Rights says that cannot happen here. The Sixth Amendment promises a *trial* that is speedy, meaning soon, and public, meaning anyone can watch. Secret trials are not allowed.

The Sixth Amendment also promises a *jury*. A jury is a group of ordinary people, usually twelve, who listen to the evidence and decide if you are guilty. They are not police or judges. They are neighbors. The amendment says you must be told exactly what you are accused of. You may see and question the people who say you did it. And you may have a lawyer to speak for you.

Other amendments help too. The Fourth says police need a good reason before they search your home. The Fifth says you cannot be forced to speak against yourself. The Eighth says punishments may not be cruel. Together, these rights mean the government must prove you did wrong. You do not have to prove you are *innocent*. A person is innocent until proven guilty.

words.d: the process in court where evidence is shown and a judge or jury decides if someone broke the law
a group of ordinary citizens who listen to a trial and decide the verdict
not guilty; a person is treated as innocent until the government proves otherwise

look.title: The Sixth Amendment Begins
look.text: In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right to a speedy and public trial, by an impartial jury of the State and district wherein the crime shall have been committed...
look.prompt: The word "impartial" means not taking sides. Why would it be unfair if a jury already took one side before the trial started?

check.q: What is a jury?
choices: A group of ordinary citizens who decide a case
check.why: A jury is made of ordinary people, usually twelve, who listen to the evidence and decide if someone is guilty.

check.q: Why must a trial be public?
choices: So the jury can charge tickets
So the judge does not have to explain
So that secret, unfair trials cannot happen
check.why: A public trial means anyone can watch. That makes it much harder to treat someone unfairly in secret.

check.q: Who must prove something in a criminal trial?
choices: The government must prove the person is guilty
The person must prove they are innocent
The jury must prove the judge is right
check.why: A person is innocent until proven guilty. The government has to prove its case.

lessons.title: Laws and Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: Citizens have responsibilities as well as rights, starting with obeying laws and paying taxes.
reading: Rights are what the government owes you. A *responsibility* is what you owe back. Think of the crosswalk again. The city painted it. But the crosswalk only works if drivers obey the law and stop. A community where nobody follows the rules is not free. It is just unsafe. So the first responsibility of every citizen is to obey the law, even laws you do not like. If you think a law is wrong, work to change it.

The second responsibility is paying *taxes*. A tax is money people pay to the government. The crosswalk cost about one thousand dollars. Where did that money come from? From taxes. When you buy a toy in Illinois, part of the price is sales tax. Adults who earn money pay income tax. People who own a house pay property tax, which pays for most of your school.

Nobody loves paying taxes. But every road, park, firefighter, library book and school lunch is paid for with them. The Constitution gives Congress and the state legislatures the power to tax. The people we elect decide how much and on what. If voters think taxes are too high, or spent badly, they can choose new leaders. That is one more reason voting matters.

words.d: something you owe or must do, such as obeying laws and paying taxes
money people pay to the government to pay for roads, schools, police and other shared things

look.title: Where the Dollars Go
look.text: A town collects tax money every year. It spends it on the fire department, the police, snow plows, the library, the parks and paving streets. The school district collects its own property taxes and spends them on teachers, buses, books and buildings. Every dollar spent on one thing cannot be spent on another.
look.prompt: If your town had to cut one thing from that list, which would hurt the most people? Which would hurt the fewest?

check.q: What is a responsibility?
choices: Something you owe or must do
check.why: A right is what the government owes you. A responsibility is what you owe back, like obeying laws.

check.q: Which tax pays for most of a public school in Illinois?
choices: Property tax on homes and land
check.why: Property tax, paid by people who own homes and land, pays for most of the public schools.

check.q: What should a citizen do about a law they think is wrong?
choices: Wait for the police to change it
Obey it while working to change it
check.why: Citizens obey the law even when they disagree. They use their rights to speak, petition and vote for a change.

lessons.title: Serving on a Jury and Voting
lessons.mainIdea: Two big responsibilities, jury duty and voting, only work when ordinary people show up.
reading: Remember the right to a jury? A jury needs jurors. That is where you come in. When you are eighteen and a citizen, your county may send you a letter. It says: report for *jury duty*. You go to the courthouse. You might be picked to sit on a jury and decide a real case. It can take a day or a week. Your employer must let you go. Jury duty is a responsibility because someone else's right to a fair trial depends on you.

Voting is a right. But it is also a responsibility. A democracy where nobody votes is not really a democracy. In many elections in Illinois, fewer than half of the people who could vote actually do. That means a small group is choosing for everyone. When you turn eighteen, register. Learn about the candidates. Then vote in every election, not just the big one for president.

Some responsibilities are not written in any law. Learning about the issues is one. Being *informed* means knowing the facts before you decide. Reading more than one news source helps. Treating people with different opinions with respect is another. A democracy runs on argument. It falls apart when people stop listening to each other.

words.d: the responsibility of a citizen to serve on a jury when called by the court
knowing the facts about something before you decide

look.title: The Letter in the Mail
look.text: Mr. Okafor gets a letter from Cook County. He must report for jury duty on Monday. He is a bus driver and would rather work. On Monday he sits with eleven strangers. They hear a case about a car crash. They talk for three hours. At the end, they all agree on the answer. The judge thanks them.
look.prompt: Mr. Okafor did not want to go. Why is it important that people like him, and not only judges, decide cases?

check.q: Why is jury duty a responsibility?
choices: Someone else's right to a fair trial depends on citizens showing up
The judge cannot work without it
check.why: A jury is made of ordinary people. If no one serves, no one can get a fair trial by jury.

check.q: What does it mean to be informed?
choices: To know the facts before you decide
To be told what to think
To be called for jury duty
check.why: An informed voter knows the facts about the issues and candidates before voting.

check.q: What happens when very few people vote?
choices: A small group chooses for everyone
check.why: If most people stay home, the few who vote decide for the whole community.

lessons.title: Speaking Up
lessons.mainIdea: Citizens have a responsibility to speak up when something is unfair or unsafe, in ways that are respectful and clear.
reading: Jonah could have said nothing after the truck skidded. It would have been easier. But then the next kid might not be so lucky. Speaking up is a responsibility because a government cannot fix problems it does not know about. Your council member does not walk to Lincoln Elementary. You do. You know things leaders do not.

Speaking up works best when it is *respectful* and *specific*. Respectful means you attack the problem, not the person. "The corner is dangerous" works. "You don't care about kids" does not. Specific means you say exactly what is wrong and what you want. The four friends did not just say Oak Street was bad. They said two hundred cars and sixty kids and no crosswalk. Numbers are hard to ignore.

Speaking up also means standing up for other people. A right that only some people have is not really a right. Later in this chapter you will meet Jane Addams and Ida B. Wells. Both were Chicago women who spoke up for people who had no power. They were not always popular. They were often right. That is what a good citizen does.

words.d: polite and fair; attacking the problem, not the person
exact and clear; saying just what is wrong and what you want

look.title: Two Ways to Say It
look.text: Message A: "This school is terrible and nobody cares. Fix the playground!" Message B: "The swing on the left side of the playground has a broken chain. Two kids fell off it last week. Can it be fixed before Friday?" Both are sent to the principal.
look.prompt: Which message is more likely to get the swing fixed? What does Message B have that Message A does not?

check.q: Why is speaking up a responsibility?
choices: Because it is required by the Sixth Amendment
Because leaders pay people to complain
Because the police will arrest you if you do not
Because a government cannot fix problems it does not know about
check.why: Leaders do not see everything. Citizens who speak up help government know what needs fixing.

check.q: Which is the most specific message?
choices: The swing on the left has a broken chain
check.why: Specific means exact. Naming the swing and the broken chain tells the principal just what to fix.

check.q: What does respectful speech mean in this lesson?
choices: Attacking the problem, not the person
check.why: Respectful means you can disagree strongly but you focus on the problem instead of insulting a person.

lessons.title: The Illinois Constitution
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has its own constitution, written in Springfield, that sets up the state government and lists its own bill of rights.
reading: The United States has a constitution. So does Illinois. A *constitution* is the written plan for a government. It says what the branches are, how leaders are chosen, and what rights the people have. Illinois became a state in 1818. Since then it has had four constitutions. The one we use now was written in 1970. It was approved by the voters of Illinois in a special election.

The Illinois Constitution starts with a preamble, an opening statement of goals. It says the people of Illinois set up this government to provide for the health, safety and welfare of the people, to keep a fair and orderly government, and to work toward justice for everyone. Then its very first article is its own bill of rights. It protects free speech, religion and fair trials, just like the U.S. Bill of Rights, and it adds some more.

One right the Illinois Constitution adds is that no one may be treated unfairly in hiring or housing because of race, religion, national origin, sex or a disability. Another is a right to a healthy environment. The Constitution also says Springfield is the *seat of government*. That is why the governor, the General Assembly and the Illinois Supreme Court all work there.

words.d: the written plan for a government: its branches, its leaders and the people's rights
the opening statement of a constitution that tells its goals
the city where a government does its work; Springfield for Illinois

look.title: What Illinois Promises Its People
look.text: The preamble of the Illinois Constitution says, in short, that the people of Illinois set up this government to provide for their health, safety and welfare, to keep a representative and orderly government, to work against poverty and unfair treatment, to give everyone a fair chance at justice, and to secure freedom for themselves and their children.
look.prompt: Pick one goal from this list. How did the crosswalk story help meet that goal?

check.q: What is a constitution?
choices: The written plan for a government
A meeting of the General Assembly
check.why: A constitution sets up the branches, tells how leaders are chosen, and lists the people's rights.

check.q: When was the current Illinois Constitution written?
check.why: Illinois has had four constitutions. The one used today was written in 1970 and approved by voters.

check.q: Which right is in the Illinois Constitution but is NOT spelled out in the U.S. Bill of Rights?
choices: The right to a healthy environment
The right to a jury trial
check.why: The Illinois Constitution adds a right to a healthy environment and protection from unfair treatment in hiring and housing.

lessons.title: Symbols of Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois uses symbols like the cardinal, the violet and the white oak to show what the state is proud of.
reading: A *symbol* is a thing that stands for something bigger. A flag stands for a country. A heart stands for love. States pick symbols too. Illinois has chosen a state bird, the cardinal, a bright red bird you can see in winter. Its state flower is the violet, a small purple flower that grows in spring. Its state tree is the white oak, which can live for hundreds of years.

Illinois has many more symbols, and most were chosen by the General Assembly after schoolchildren asked for them. The state animal is the white-tailed deer. The state insect is the monarch butterfly, which flies through Illinois on its way to Mexico each fall. The state fish is the bluegill. The state prairie grass is big bluestem, which once covered most of the state. The state snack is popcorn.

The state flag shows the Illinois seal: an eagle on a rock holding a banner with the state *motto*, "State Sovereignty, National Union." A motto is a short saying about what a place believes. The words mean Illinois governs itself but is part of one nation. The state's nickname is the Prairie State, because of the tall grass that once covered it. License plates say "Land of Lincoln," for Abraham Lincoln, who lived in Springfield before he became president.

words.d: a thing that stands for something bigger, like a flag standing for a country
a short saying about what a place or group believes

look.title: Choose a New Symbol
look.text: Most Illinois symbols were chosen after students wrote to the General Assembly. Fourth graders helped make the monarch butterfly the state insect. Other students pushed for popcorn as the state snack. Now imagine your class wants a state symbol for something Illinois does not have yet, like a state sandwich or a state sound.
look.prompt: What would you propose, and what would you write to your state representative to convince them?

check.q: What is the state bird of Illinois?
check.why: The cardinal, a red bird seen even in winter, is the state bird. The monarch is the state insect.

check.q: What does the Illinois motto "State Sovereignty, National Union" mean?
choices: Illinois wants to leave the United States
Illinois has no government of its own
Illinois governs itself but is part of one nation
Illinois is the most important state
check.why: Sovereignty means self-rule. Union means being joined together. Illinois rules itself and belongs to the nation.

check.q: Why is Illinois called the Prairie State?
choices: Because tall prairie grass once covered most of it
check.why: Before farms, tall grasses like big bluestem covered most of Illinois. That is the prairie.

lessons.title: Petitions, Letters, Meetings
lessons.mainIdea: To change something, find out who decides, gather evidence, and then ask in writing and in person.
reading: The four friends did not get a crosswalk by wishing. They followed steps that work for almost any change. First, find out who is in charge. A city street belongs to the city. A state highway belongs to the state. A school rule belongs to the principal or the school board. Asking the wrong person wastes time. Second, gather *evidence*. Evidence is facts that support what you say. The car count was evidence.

Third, put it in writing. A petition shows that many people want the same thing. A letter or email tells one leader exactly what you want and why. Keep it short. Say who you are, what the problem is, what you want done, and what your evidence is. Sign your name. Leaders get many letters. Polite, clear ones with facts stand out.

Fourth, show up. Every city council, village board and school board holds *public meetings*. There is usually a time called public comment when anyone may speak for a few minutes. It is scary the first time. Luis found that out. But leaders remember a real kid at the microphone longer than a letter. Fifth, follow up. Ask what happened. Say thank you when it gets done. That makes the next request easier.

words.d: facts that support what you say, like a count of cars
a meeting of a government board that anyone may attend and often speak at

look.title: The Crosswalk Numbers
rows: Cars each morning at the corner
Cost of the crosswalk in dollars
look.prompt: Which of these numbers would matter most to a council member worried about safety? Which would matter most to one worried about money?

check.q: What is the first step to making a change?
choices: Find out who is in charge of the problem
Wait for an adult to notice
check.why: A street belongs to the city, a highway to the state, a school rule to the principal. Ask the right person.

check.q: What makes a letter to a leader stand out?
choices: Being short, polite, clear and full of facts
Being at least ten pages long
check.why: Leaders get many letters. Short, respectful, specific letters with evidence are the ones that get read.

check.q: What is public comment at a meeting?
choices: A time when anyone may speak for a few minutes
A time when reporters ask questions
check.why: Most boards set aside time at each public meeting for citizens to speak briefly.

lessons.title: Volunteering
lessons.mainIdea: Volunteering means giving your time to help your community, and it is one of the strongest ways to make a change.
reading: Not every change needs a law. Some things you can just do. To *volunteer* means to give your time and work for free to help others. Picking up trash in a park, reading to younger kids, packing food boxes at a food bank, or shoveling snow for an older neighbor are all volunteering. Nobody pays you. You do it because the community is yours.

Volunteers do work that government cannot always do. In Illinois, thousands of people give time to food pantries, animal shelters, hospitals, libraries and youth sports. When floods hit river towns along the Mississippi and Illinois rivers, volunteers fill sandbags side by side with government crews. A town with many volunteers is stronger and friendlier than a town with few.

Volunteering also teaches you things a book cannot. You see the problem close up. You meet the people it affects. Many people who go on to run for office started by volunteering. The four friends might not have cared about Oak Street if they had not walked it every day. Being there is the first step to caring. Caring is the first step to changing.

words.d: to give your time and work for free to help others
a place that collects and gives out food to people who need it

look.title: A Saturday Morning
look.text: On one Saturday in a Chicago neighborhood, a group of teens plants flowers in a vacant lot. Down the block, a retired teacher tutors two kids at the library. At the food pantry, a family sorts cans. None of them is paid. By noon, the lot is green, the kids have finished their homework, and forty families have food.
look.prompt: Which of these three jobs could a government have done? Which one might a government have done worse than the volunteers?

check.q: What does it mean to volunteer?
choices: To be elected to a council
To give your time and work for free to help others
check.why: Volunteers work without pay to help their community, like packing food boxes or picking up litter.

check.q: Which is an example of volunteering?
choices: Shoveling an older neighbor's sidewalk for free
Buying a snack at the store
check.why: Volunteering is unpaid help for others. Shoveling for a neighbor without pay fits.

check.q: Why do many people who run for office start as volunteers?
choices: Because volunteers see problems close up and start to care
Because volunteers get paid more later
Because you cannot vote unless you volunteer
check.why: Being there is the first step to caring. Volunteers meet the people a problem affects.

lessons.title: Jane Addams and Hull House
lessons.mainIdea: Jane Addams used her rights to speak up for poor families in Chicago and helped win laws that protected children.
reading: In 1889, a young woman named Jane Addams moved into an old brick house on Halsted Street in Chicago. The neighborhood was crowded with families who had just come from Italy, Germany, Poland and other countries. Many were poor. Children worked in factories instead of going to school. Garbage piled up in the alleys. Addams and her friend Ellen Gates Starr named the house Hull House and opened its doors.

Hull House became a place where neighbors could learn English, take art classes, get child care, and find help. But Addams did more than help one family at a time. She used her rights. She counted the garbage that the city failed to pick up and complained until the city made her a garbage inspector for the ward. She spoke and wrote against *child labor*, meaning young children working long hours in factories. She pushed for the first playgrounds and for a special court for young people.

Addams also spoke against war, which made her unpopular with many Americans for a time. She kept speaking. In 1931 she became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. She died in 1935. Her work shows what one citizen can do with the rights to speak, write, petition and assemble. Hull House still stands on Halsted Street as a museum.

words.d: the house on Halsted Street in Chicago where Jane Addams helped immigrant families, opened in 1889
young children working long hours in factories or other jobs instead of going to school
a famous prize given each year to a person who works for peace

look.title: Addams on Why She Stayed
look.text: In her book about Hull House, Jane Addams explained that she did not move to Halsted Street only to help the poor. She believed that well-off young people needed the neighborhood as much as the neighborhood needed them. Living among people with real problems, she said, gave her life a purpose that books and travel never had.
look.cite: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House, 1910 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Addams said she needed her neighbors as much as they needed her. What might she have meant?

check.q: What was Hull House?
choices: A place in Chicago where Jane Addams helped immigrant families
check.why: Jane Addams opened Hull House on Halsted Street in 1889 to help poor immigrant neighbors.

check.q: Which problem did Addams work to end?
check.why: Addams spoke and wrote against child labor and helped win laws that protected children.

check.q: What prize did Jane Addams win in 1931?
check.why: In 1931 Addams became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

lessons.title: Ida B. Wells Tells the Truth
lessons.mainIdea: Ida B. Wells used freedom of the press to expose violence against Black Americans and helped win the vote for women in Illinois.
reading: Ida B. Wells was born in Mississippi in 1862, during the Civil War, to parents who were enslaved. She grew up free, became a teacher, and then a newspaper writer in Memphis, Tennessee. In 1892, three of her friends, Black men who owned a grocery store, were dragged from jail and killed by a mob. No one was punished. This crime, killing a person without a trial, is called *lynching*.

Wells did what a free press is for. She gathered the facts. She counted lynchings across the South and printed the numbers and names. She showed that the excuses given for the killings were lies. Angry men destroyed her newspaper office. She could not go back to Memphis. She kept writing anyway, and she carried her *investigation* to the North and to England.

In the 1890s Wells settled in Chicago. She married a lawyer named Ferdinand Barnett and raised four children. She helped start the NAACP in 1909, a group that still fights for equal rights. In 1913 she founded the Alpha Suffrage Club, the first group in Illinois to organize Black women to vote. That same year Illinois let women vote for president, the first state east of the Mississippi to do so. Wells died in 1931. Today a Chicago street carries her name.

words.d: killing a person by a mob without any trial
careful work to find out the facts about something
the right to vote

look.title: Wells on Truth
look.text: Ida B. Wells said that the way to right wrongs is to shine the light of truth on them. She believed that once people saw the facts, they could no longer pretend the wrongs were not happening.
look.prompt: Wells fought with numbers and names instead of weapons. Why can facts be so powerful against injustice?

check.q: Which freedom did Ida B. Wells use most in her fight?
check.why: Wells was a journalist. She printed the facts about lynching even after her office was destroyed.

check.q: What is lynching?
choices: A fair trial with a jury
Killing a person by a mob without a trial
A vote by the city council
check.why: Lynching is when a mob kills someone without any trial. Wells's friends were killed this way in 1892.

check.q: What did the Alpha Suffrage Club do?
choices: Organized Black women in Illinois to vote
check.why: Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in 1913 to help Black women in Illinois use their new right to vote.

review.q: The Bill of Rights was added to the Constitution in what year?
review.why: The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791.

review.q: Which of these is a First Amendment freedom?
choices: The right to a speedy trial
The right to vote at eighteen
The right to own a house
review.why: The First Amendment protects religion, speech, press, assembly and petition.

review.q: In a criminal trial, who decides if a person is guilty when there is a jury?
review.why: The jury, a group of ordinary citizens, listens to the evidence and decides.

review.q: Which is a responsibility, not a right?
review.why: Rights are what the government owes you. Paying taxes is something citizens owe back.

review.q: Where is the seat of the Illinois government?
review.why: The Illinois Constitution names Springfield as the seat of government.

review.q: What is the Illinois state flower?
review.why: The violet, a small purple spring flower, is the Illinois state flower.

review.q: In the crosswalk story, why did the four friends count cars before asking for a change?
choices: To gather evidence that would convince the council
To find out who owned the street
Because counting cars is a school rule
review.why: Evidence is facts that support what you say. The car count made their request hard to ignore.

review.q: What did Jane Addams and Ida B. Wells have in common?
choices: Both used their rights to speak up for people who had little power
Both served on the Supreme Court
review.why: Addams spoke for poor immigrant families. Wells spoke for Black Americans and for women's votes. Both used free speech and press.
